title: New model identifies priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile
excerpt: Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.
content_html:
Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.

The loss and degradation of native ecosystems not only threaten biodiversity but also undermine the benefits people receive from nature, such as climate regulation and the availability and quality of water. Against this backdrop, ecological restoration plays a key role in recovering ecosystems and the functions they provide.

"However, these processes require financial and human resources, as well as time, all of which are limited. Identifying where to focus restoration efforts and how to make the best use of available resources has therefore become a key challenge," explains Jessica Castillo-Mandujano, a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) and co-author of a recent study published in Journal of Environmental Management.

The study focused on developing a tool to identify and prioritize areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, taking multiple ecological objectives into account simultaneously. The research was led by Matías Moreno-Faguett, an industrial civil engineer from the University of Talca and an associate researcher at the Forest Science and Technology Centre of Catalonia.

The study involved several researchers from the IEB and other institutions, including María José Martínez Harms, Bárbara Larraín, Olga Barbosa, Cecilia Smith, Aníbal Pauchard, Eduardo Álvarez Miranda, Eduardo Fuentes Lillo, Micaela Poutay and Patricio Pliscoff.

Reducing the risk of species extinction, prioritizing carbon stocks, promoting the restoration of riparian areas and assessing the ecological feasibility of restoration processes are the four objectives integrated into this multiobjective model. According to its lead author, who is completing his doctorate in the Mathematics Program at the University of Seville, the tool is intended to support future planning decisions.

"Chile has many restoration initiatives, but they tend to be quite fragmented. We therefore set out to look at the country as a whole, taking into account its wide diversity of climates and ecosystems. This also means recognizing that different areas have different protection needs. Protecting and restoring ecosystems in the Atacama Desert is very different from doing so in the fjords of Patagonia," explains Álvarez, an industrial civil engineer, professor at the University of Talca and IEB researcher.

Four objectives to guide restoration

To develop the model, the research team worked with spatial data covering continental Chile, dividing the territory into 812,910 planning units, each measuring 1 square kilometer (0.39 square miles). Using mathematical optimization, they integrated the four ecological criteria to assess different restoration benefits and priorities.

Castillo emphasizes the importance of developing this model, as priority areas may vary depending on the objectives being pursued. "We seek to recover biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, but also the contributions we receive from nature, which are essential to human well-being. Restoration must therefore also take into account the social, economic and cultural dimensions of each territory. However, an area that is important for biodiversity recovery is not necessarily the same area that should be prioritized to address a social need. That is why these objectives must be considered together when planning restoration."

According to the authors, one of the study's major contributions is the inclusion of ecological feasibility. This concept refers to the conditions that help ensure that ecosystem recovery can be sustained over time. "An area may be extremely important for biodiversity conservation but also be exposed to threats that make its recovery more difficult," explains Castillo.

In this context, the researcher highlights three factors considered in the assessment of ecological feasibility: exposure to recurrent wildfires, human pressure associated with the presence of roads and infrastructure, and the potential presence of invasive species.

The computational model also makes it possible to compare different scenarios and observe how priorities change when one or more criteria are included or excluded. "We can add or remove elements and see what happens. In this study, we examined what happens when ecological feasibility is taken into account and what happens when it is not," says Moreno.

One of the findings was that including ecological feasibility as an objective changes the areas identified as priorities. In an illustrative scenario covering a planning area equivalent to 30% of the national territory, the model replaced 16.52% of the planning units selected in the solution without this criterion with other areas when ecological feasibility was incorporated.

This change improved the performance of the ecological feasibility and species extinction risk reduction objectives, although it reduced the performance of the carbon stock and riparian restoration objectives. The findings show that different restoration objectives do not always converge on the same locations and that prioritization involves assessing the benefits that restoration efforts are intended to achieve.

"The selected sites are, for example, located farther away from areas affected by wildfires, places under anthropogenic pressure or areas with invasive species. Some were selected because they contribute to several objectives, while others do not. The question is: what characteristics do these sites share, and what patterns can we identify? That was one of the issues we discussed during the project," adds Moreno.

Another finding was the identification of areas that contribute simultaneously to more than one ecological objective. In fact, 80.4% of the selected planning units were classified as multifunctional, making it possible to identify where different priorities overlap and to better guide decisions about where to focus restoration efforts.

Different regions, different contributions

Chile is home to a wide diversity of ecosystems, ranging from northern deserts to temperate forests and southernmost ecosystems, each with its own ecological characteristics and threats.

In this context, the findings show that restoration priorities differ across the country's major geographic regions. In the north, a significant proportion of the selected sites contribute to the ecological feasibility objective, due to the lower prevalence of threats such as wildfires and invasive species. In central Chile, areas that contribute to reducing the risk of species extinction become more important, given the greater human pressure on this region and threats such as wildfires and invasive alien species. Farther south, sites with larger carbon stocks stand out.

"What is needed in the north is different from what is needed in the south, because these are different ecosystems. In the north, flora and fauna can be extremely fragile, so efforts should focus on protecting them. In central Chile, we have many species that are unique to the country, but also a greater human population and more threats from wildfires and invasive species. In the south, carbon is particularly important because of the presence of wetlands, fjords, forests and peatlands," says Álvarez.

Supporting decision-making

The researchers emphasize that the model is intended to provide information to guide planning and support better-informed decisions. Its results do not necessarily constitute an intervention plan that is ready for implementation. Implementation also requires local information, cost assessments, land tenure conditions and the participation of relevant stakeholders.

"The tools we have developed are intended to support decision-making and to be used in discussions and reflection as part of a broader process. Ideally, the map would be examined together with specialists. It is also important to involve communities, political stakeholders, Indigenous peoples and other groups," says Moreno.

"The main contribution of this research is to provide a tool for strategically planning ecological restoration by identifying the areas that best meet the objectives we aim to achieve. This is particularly important given the environmental and climate emergency and the limited resources available for restoration," explains Castillo.

The authors also highlight the flexibility of the methodology, which makes it possible to incorporate more detailed and up-to-date spatial information, as well as new objectives and constraints, to adapt planning to the conditions of each territory. Nevertheless, the quality of the recommendations will always depend on the available data and their validation in the context in which the tool is applied.

"This is precisely the kind of research that should inform public policy, because it has a fairly concrete application and clearly defined objectives that can help develop a plan. With the necessary adjustments, it could become a valuable resource for the Biodiversity and Protected Areas Service (SBAP) to support its decision-making. Now that we have this new institutional framework and the international commitments we have undertaken, it is important that conservation decisions be based on appropriate information," concludes Álvarez.

Publication details

Matías Moreno-Faguett et al., Balancing ecological benefits and feasibility in large-scale restoration planning: A multi-objective optimization decision-support framework, Journal of Environmental Management (2026). DOI: 10.1016/j.jenvman.2026.131246

content_html_zh:
Researchers from Chile's Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) have developed a multiobjective model to identify priority areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, South America. The tool integrates four ecological objectives: reducing species extinction risk, prioritizing carbon stocks, restoring riparian areas and assessing ecological feasibility. The findings show that including ecological feasibility changes restoration priorities, while 80.4% of the selected areas contribute to more than one ecological objective. By identifying areas where different priorities overlap, the model can help guide strategic restoration planning and support better-informed conservation decisions amid growing environmental challenges and limited resources.

The loss and degradation of native ecosystems not only threaten biodiversity but also undermine the benefits people receive from nature, such as climate regulation and the availability and quality of water. Against this backdrop, ecological restoration plays a key role in recovering ecosystems and the functions they provide.

"However, these processes require financial and human resources, as well as time, all of which are limited. Identifying where to focus restoration efforts and how to make the best use of available resources has therefore become a key challenge," explains Jessica Castillo-Mandujano, a postdoctoral researcher at the Institute of Ecology and Biodiversity (IEB) and co-author of a recent study published in Journal of Environmental Management.

The study focused on developing a tool to identify and prioritize areas for large-scale ecological restoration in Chile, taking multiple ecological objectives into account simultaneously. The research was led by Matías Moreno-Faguett, an industrial civil engineer from the University of Talca and an associate researcher at the Forest Science and Technology Centre of Catalonia.

The study involved several researchers from the IEB and other institutions, including María José Martínez Harms, Bárbara Larraín, Olga Barbosa, Cecilia Smith, Aníbal Pauchard, Eduardo Álvarez Miranda, Eduardo Fuentes Lillo, Micaela Poutay and Patricio Pliscoff.

Reducing the risk of species extinction, prioritizing carbon stocks, promoting the restoration of riparian areas and assessing the ecological feasibility of restoration processes are the four objectives integrated into this multiobjective model. According to its lead author, who is completing his doctorate in the Mathematics Program at the University of Seville, the tool is intended to support future planning decisions.

"Chile has many restoration initiatives, but they tend to be quite fragmented. We therefore set out to look at the country as a whole, taking into account its wide diversity of climates and ecosystems. This also means recognizing that different areas have different protection needs. Protecting and restoring ecosystems in the Atacama Desert is very different from doing so in the fjords of Patagonia," explains Álvarez, an industrial civil engineer, professor at the University of Talca and IEB researcher.

Four objectives to guide restoration

To develop the model, the research team worked with spatial data covering continental Chile, dividing the territory into 812,910 planning units, each measuring 1 square kilometer (0.39 square miles). Using mathematical optimization, they integrated the four ecological criteria to assess different restoration benefits and priorities.

Castillo emphasizes the importance of developing this model, as priority areas may vary depending on the objectives being pursued. "We seek to recover biodiversity and ecosystem functioning, but also the contributions we receive from nature, which are essential to human well-being. Restoration must therefore also take into account the social, economic and cultural dimensions of each territory. However, an area that is important for biodiversity recovery is not necessarily the same area that should be prioritized to address a social need. That is why these objectives must be considered together when planning restoration."

According to the authors, one of the study's major contributions is the inclusion of ecological feasibility. This concept refers to the conditions that help ensure that ecosystem recovery can be sustained over time. "An area may be extremely important for biodiversity conservation but also be exposed to threats that make its recovery more difficult," explains Castillo.

In this context, the researcher highlights three factors considered in the assessment of ecological feasibility: exposure to recurrent wildfires, human pressure associated with the presence of roads and infrastructure, and the potential presence of invasive species.

The computational model also makes it possible to compare different scenarios and observe how priorities change when one or more criteria are included or excluded. "We can add or remove elements and see what happens. In this study, we examined what happens when ecological feasibility is taken into account and what happens when it is not," says Moreno.

One of the findings was that including ecological feasibility as an objective changes the areas identified as priorities. In an illustrative scenario covering a planning area equivalent to 30% of the national territory, the model replaced 16.52% of the planning units selected in the solution without this criterion with other areas when ecological feasibility was incorporated.

This change improved the performance of the ecological feasibility and species extinction risk reduction objectives, although it reduced the performance of the carbon stock and riparian restoration objectives. The findings show that different restoration objectives do not always converge on the same locations and that prioritization involves assessing the benefits that restoration efforts are intended to achieve.

"The selected sites are, for example, located farther away from areas affected by wildfires, places under anthropogenic pressure or areas with invasive species. Some were selected because they contribute to several objectives, while others do not. The question is: what characteristics do these sites share, and what patterns can we identify? That was one of the issues we discussed during the project," adds Moreno.

Another finding was the identification of areas that contribute simultaneously to more than one ecological objective. In fact, 80.4% of the selected planning units were classified as multifunctional, making it possible to identify where different priorities overlap and to better guide decisions about where to focus restoration efforts.

Different regions, different contributions

Chile is home to a wide diversity of ecosystems, ranging from northern deserts to temperate forests and southernmost ecosystems, each with its own ecological characteristics and threats.

In this context, the findings show that restoration priorities differ across the country's major geographic regions. In the north, a significant proportion of the selected sites contribute to the ecological feasibility objective, due to the lower prevalence of threats such as wildfires and invasive species. In central Chile, areas that contribute to reducing the risk of species extinction become more important, given the greater human pressure on this region and threats such as wildfires and invasive alien species. Farther south, sites with larger carbon stocks stand out.

"What is needed in the north is different from what is needed in the south, because these are different ecosystems. In the north, flora and fauna can be extremely fragile, so efforts should focus on protecting them. In central Chile, we have many species that are unique to the country, but also a greater human population and more threats from wildfires and invasive species. In the south, carbon is particularly important because of the presence of wetlands, fjords, forests and peatlands," says Álvarez.

Supporting decision-making

The researchers emphasize that the model is intended to provide information to guide planning and support better-informed decisions. Its results do not necessarily constitute an intervention plan that is ready for implementation. Implementation also requires local information, cost assessments, land tenure conditions and the participation of relevant stakeholders.

"The tools we have developed are intended to support decision-making and to be used in discussions and reflection as part of a broader process. Ideally, the map would be examined together with specialists. It is also important to involve communities, political stakeholders, Indigenous peoples and other groups," says Moreno.

"The main contribution of this research is to provide a tool for strategically planning ecological restoration by identifying the areas that best meet the objectives we aim to achieve. This is particularly important given the environmental and climate emergency and the limited resources available for restoration," explains Castillo.

The authors also highlight the flexibility of the methodology, which makes it possible to incorporate more detailed and up-to-date spatial information, as well as new objectives and constraints, to adapt planning to the conditions of each territory. Nevertheless, the quality of the recommendations will always depend on the available data and their validation in the context in which the tool is applied.

"This is precisely the kind of research that should inform public policy, because it has a fairly concrete application and clearly defined objectives that can help develop a plan. With the necessary adjustments, it could become a valuable resource for the Biodiversity and Protected Areas Service (SBAP) to support its decision-making. Now that we have this new institutional framework and the international commitments we have undertaken, it is important that conservation decisions be based on appropriate information," concludes Álvarez.
